{{Legend0|#D3D3D3|No election}} }} '''United States gubernatorial elections''' were held on November 6, 2018, in 36 states and three territories. These elections formed part of the [[2018 United States elections]]. Other coinciding elections were the [[2018 United States Senate elections]] and the [[2018 United States House of Representatives elections]]. Many of the states holding gubernatorial elections [[Term limits in the United States#Gubernatorial term limits|have term limits]] which made some multi-term governors ineligible for re-election. Two [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governors were term-limited while six incumbent Democratic governors were eligible for re-election. Among [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governors, twelve were term-limited while eleven could seek re-election. One [[Independent politician|independent]] governor was eligible for re-election. Elections were held in 26 of the 33 states with Republican governors, nine of the 16 states with Democratic governors, one state (Alaska) with an independent governor, two territories (Guam and Northern Mariana Islands) with Republican governors, one territory (U.S. Virgin Islands) with an independent governor, and the District of Columbia with a Democratic mayor. Incumbent state governors running to be reelected included 14 Republicans, five Democrats, and one independent. Territorial incumbents running included one Republican and one independent. The incumbent Democratic mayor of Washington, D.C. also ran for re-election. Democrats gained control of nine state and territorial governorships that had previously been held by Republicans and an independent. They picked up Republican-held open seats in the states of [[2018 Kansas gubernatorial election|Kansas]], [[2018 Maine gubernatorial election|Maine]], [[2018 Michigan gubernatorial election|Michigan]], [[2018 Nevada gubernatorial election|Nevada]], and [[2018 New Mexico gubernatorial election|New Mexico]], in addition to defeating Republican incumbents in [[2018 Illinois gubernatorial election|Illinois]] and [[2018 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|Wisconsin]] and not losing any seats of their own. Additionally, they won the Republican-controlled territory of [[2018 Guamanian gubernatorial election|Guam]] and the independent-controlled territory of the [[2018 United States Virgin Islands gubernatorial election|U.S. Virgin Islands]]. Republicans won the governorship of [[2018 Alaska gubernatorial election|Alaska]] previously held by an independent.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/11/06/us/elections/results-governor-elections.html|title=Governor Election Results: Democrats Retake Several States|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=November 6, 2018|access-date=December 11, 2018|archive-date=December 10, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181210190801/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/11/06/us/elections/results-governor-elections.html|url-status=live}} Democrats also won the total popular vote for the year's gubernatorial elections for the second year in a row. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last time that Republicans won governorships in Arizona, Maryland, and Massachusetts. Six [[List of female governors in the United States|women won election for the first time as Governor]] in 2018. == Election predictions == Several sites and individuals publish predictions of competitive seats. These predictions look at factors such as the strength of the incumbent (if the incumbent is running for re-election), the strength of the candidates, and the partisan leanings of the state (reflected in part by the state's [[Cook Partisan Voting Index]] rating). The predictions assign ratings to each seat, with the rating indicating the predicted advantage that a party has in winning that seat. Most election predictors use "tossup" to indicate that neither party has an advantage, "lean" to indicate that one party has a slight advantage, "likely" or "favored" to indicate that one party has a significant but not insurmountable advantage and "safe" or "solid" to indicate that one party has a near-certain chance of victory. Some predictions also include a "tilt" rating that indicates that one party has an advantage that is not quite as strong as the "lean" rating would indicate (except Fox News, where "likely" is the highest rating given). LePage won re-election in a three-way race over Democrat [[Mike Michaud]] and independent [[Eliot Cutler]], [[Maine gubernatorial election, 2014|in 2014]]. The primary election was June 12, and conducted with [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked choice voting]], a system recently implemented and being used for the first time in the [[2018 Maine elections|2018 elections in Maine]]. It was not used in the general election due to an [[advisory opinion]] by the [[Maine Supreme Judicial Court]] calling its use in general elections for state offices unconstitutional. Businessman and [[Maine gubernatorial election, 2010|2010]] independent candidate for governor [[Shawn Moody]] won the Republican nomination. The Democratic nominee was [[Maine Attorney General|Attorney General]] [[Janet T. Mills|Janet Mills]]. Two independent candidates qualified for the ballot; [[Maine State Treasurer|State Treasurer]] [[Terry Hayes (politician)|Terry Hayes]] and businessman and newspaper columnist Alan Caron.
